title: Composition, intermediate fields, blocks, and the off-diagonal curve
summary: Functional decomposition is equivalent to an intermediate-field obstruction; double transitivity additionally detects irreducibility of \(Q_f(X,Y)=(f(X)-f(Y))/(X-Y)\).
scope: Let \(f\in\mathbb C[X]\) have degree \(n\ge2\), and let \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(f(X)-t/\mathbb C(t))\) act on its \(n\) roots. The critical-value implication additionally assumes at least two distinct critical points.

edges.label: First hypothesis
edges.explanation: The distinct roots of the derivative include at least two points; no simplicity assumption is imposed.

edges.label: Second hypothesis
edges.explanation: Different critical points have different images under the polynomial.

edges.label: Critical-value criterion
edges.explanation: Together these hypotheses imply double transitivity by the published Proposition 3.8.

edges.label: Point-stabilizer orbits
edges.explanation: Double transitivity is equivalent to irreducibility of \(Q_f(X,Y)\) over \(\mathbb C\).

edges.label: Stronger group property
edges.explanation: Every doubly transitive permutation group is primitive.

edges.label: Galois correspondence
edges.explanation: The root stabilizer is maximal exactly when \(\mathbb C(f(x))\subset\mathbb C(x)\) has no proper intermediate field.

edges.label: Polynomial Lüroth theorem
edges.explanation: A proper intermediate field is \(\mathbb C(h(x))\) for a decomposition \(f=g\circ h\) with both degrees greater than one.

sources.locator: §3, correspondence before §3.1; Lemma 3.2 and its proof

sources.note: Published numbering. The earlier arXiv version 1601.07316v1 has different theorem numbers.

body:
Write \(f=g\circ h\), identifying right components \(h\) up to postcomposition by an invertible affine polynomial. These components correspond to the fields \(\mathbb C(f(x))\subseteq\mathbb C(h(x))\subseteq\mathbb C(x)\), and to blocks containing a chosen root in the monodromy action. A block is a nonempty root subset whose translates are either equal or disjoint. Thus \(f\) has no decomposition with \(\deg g,\deg h>1\) exactly when \(G\) is primitive.

The stronger condition is a separate equivalence:

\[G\text{ doubly transitive}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q_f(X,Y)=\frac{f(X)-f(Y)}{X-Y}\text{ irreducible in }\mathbb C[X,Y].\]

Indeed, the stabilizer of one root must act transitively on all remaining roots. Kreso–Tichy, Proposition 3.8, supplies a sufficient condition: \(f'\) has at least two distinct roots, and \(f(a)\ne f(b)\) for every pair of distinct critical points \(a,b\). Multiple roots of \(f'\) are allowed.

The converse from primitivity to double transitivity fails: \(f(X)=X^5\) is indecomposable, but its geometric monodromy is cyclic of order five and \(Q_f=\prod_{\zeta^5=1,\,\zeta\ne1}(X-\zeta Y)\). This example also shows why the condition on the number of critical points cannot be dropped. The coefficient field here is \(\mathbb C\); arithmetic and geometric monodromy over a nonclosed field require separate treatment.

title: Morse geometry and Hilbert specialization require two different inputs
summary: Simple critical points and distinct critical values yield regular \(S_n\)-monodromy; the Hilbert property then supplies infinitely many specializations with the same group.
scope: Let \(K\) be a number field, \(f\in K[X]\) monic of degree \(n\ge2\), and \(t\) transcendental. Critical points are taken over \(\overline K\).

edges.label: First Morse condition
edges.explanation: The derivative has exactly \(n-1\) distinct roots over \(\overline K\).

edges.label: Second Morse condition
edges.explanation: The images of those critical points are pairwise distinct.

edges.label: Simple branching
edges.explanation: Each finite branch inertia group is generated by a transposition, and their conjugates generate geometric monodromy.

edges.label: Connected transposition action
edges.explanation: The polynomial cover is transitive, so generation by transpositions yields geometric and arithmetic group \(S_n\), with constant field \(K\).

edges.label: Generic Galois input
edges.explanation: The splitting field is regular over the coefficient field and has full symmetric group.

edges.label: Arithmetic input
edges.explanation: The affine line over a number field has the Hilbert property.

edges.label: Hilbert irreducibility
edges.explanation: Outside a thin subset of \(K\), the polynomial \(f(X)-a\) is irreducible with Galois group \(S_n\).

edges.label: Regular Hilbert specialization
edges.explanation: Regularity and the Hilbert property jointly allow specializations linearly disjoint from any prescribed finite extension, and hence infinitely many linearly disjoint splitting fields.

sources.locator: Theorems 4.4.1 and 4.4.5; Lemma 4.4.4; Proposition 4.4.6, printed pp. 39–41

body:
A polynomial is Morse when the \(n-1\) roots of \(f'\) are simple and have pairwise distinct images. Under the displayed assumptions, the splitting field \(L\) of \(f(X)-t\) satisfies

\[\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(t))=S_n,\qquad L\cap\overline K=K.\]

The proof first works geometrically. Each finite branch point contributes a transposition, and these inertia groups and their conjugates generate the transitive monodromy group. Hence that group is \(S_n\). Arithmetic monodromy lies between geometric monodromy and \(S_n\), so they coincide and regularity follows.

Hilbert irreducibility adds a different input: because \(K\) is a number field, there is a thin set \(E\subset K\) such that every \(a\in K\setminus E\) gives an irreducible \(f(X)-a\) with group \(S_n\). Regularity further permits infinitely many splitting fields that are linearly disjoint. These conclusions concern suitable specializations; the exceptional set need not be finite.

For example, \(f=X^3-X\) is Morse. At \(a=0\), its fiber splits completely; at \(a=1\), \(X^3-X-1\) is irreducible by the rational-root test and has nonsquare discriminant \(-23\), so its group is \(S_3\). The two fibers illustrate why a generic monodromy theorem alone does not certify a chosen arithmetic fiber.

title: A complete proposed classification of reducible f(X) − g(Y)
summary: The 2026 DLS preprint claims an if-and-only-if classification over \(\mathbb C\), including decomposable polynomials: common outer factors, the exact six exceptional families, or the signed quartic Chebyshev pair.
scope: Let \(f,g\in\mathbb C[X]\) have degree greater than one. The classification is Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2603.27728v1 (29 March 2026), recorded as a preprint claim.

edges.label: Case 1
edges.explanation: There exist nonconstant \(u,v\) and \(h\) of degree at least two with \(f=h\circ u\) and \(g=h\circ v\).

edges.label: Case 2
edges.explanation: There are nonconstant \(u,v\), affine \(\mu\), and an exact pair \((h_1,h_2)\) from Cassou–Noguès–Couveignes §5 with \(f=\mu\circ h_1\circ u\), \(g=\mu\circ h_2\circ v\).

edges.label: Case 3
edges.explanation: There are nonconstant \(u,v\) and affine \(\mu\) with \(f=\mu\circ T_4\circ u\), \(g=\mu\circ(-T_4)\circ v\), where \(T_4=X^4-4X^2+2\).

edges.label: Claimed exhaustive iff
edges.explanation: The preprint asserts that the union of the three displayed cases is necessary and sufficient for reducibility over the complex numbers.

edges.label: Curve interpretation
edges.explanation: Reducibility of the separated polynomial is equivalent to reducibility of the fiber product of the two polynomial maps to the projective line.

edges.label: Galois analysis
edges.explanation: The proof translates the fiber product into monodromy actions and studies kernels along polynomial decompositions.

edges.label: Exhaustiveness argument
edges.explanation: The preprint combines its solvable-case analysis with the established exceptional pairs to rule out additional minimal cases.

sources.note: Full complex classification is a preprint claim; the arithmetic Hilbert–Siegel application has additional hypotheses.
These are explicit coefficient families, not arbitrary pairs whose degrees lie in the six-number list.

sources.locator: Theorem 4.1; Theorem 5.1; Theorem 6.1 and its proof, version 1

body:
Preprint claim, exact scope. Behajaina–König–Neftin, Theorem 1.1, states that \(f(X)-g(Y)\) is reducible over \(\mathbb C\) exactly when at least one of the following occurs. All inner polynomials \(u,v\) are nonconstant; \(\mu(X)=aX+b\) has \(a\ne0\).

  1. \(f=h\circ u\) and \(g=h\circ v\), with \(\deg h\ge2\).
  2. \(f=\mu\circ h_1\circ u\) and \(g=\mu\circ h_2\circ v\), for an exact exceptional pair \((h_1,h_2)\) in Cassou–Noguès–Couveignes, §5.
  3. \(f=\mu\circ T_4\circ u\) and \(g=\mu\circ(-T_4)\circ v\), with \(T_4=X^4-4X^2+2\).

Case 2 refers to the coefficient formulas, parameter families, and coefficient conjugations in the following source locations; the degrees alone are not a criterion.

DegreeExact exceptional family
7§5.1, p. 310
11§5.2, p. 310
13§5.3, p. 311
15§5.4, pp. 311–312
21§5.5, pp. 312–313
31§5.6, pp. 313–315

The normalization satisfies \(T_m(z+z^{-1})=z^m+z^{-m}\). Case 3 is visible directly:

\[T_4(X)+T_4(Y)=(X^2+Y^2-2+\sqrt2XY)(X^2+Y^2-2-\sqrt2XY).\]

The claimed advance is exhaustiveness for arbitrary decomposable pairs. It does not by itself classify reducible arithmetic fibers \(f(X)-a\), whose Hilbert–Siegel analysis is a separate, more restricted result.

title: Rabin’s criterion: a complete finite-field irreducibility certificate
summary: One Frobenius congruence and gcd tests at the maximal proper divisors of the degree give a necessary and sufficient test, and a certified construction of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\).
scope: Let \(q\) be any prime power and \(f\in\mathbb F_q[X]\) monic of degree \(n\ge1\). The gcd conditions range over every distinct prime divisor \(\ell\mid n\); for \(n=1\) this list is empty.

edges.label: Interpret first test
edges.explanation: The congruence \(X^{q^n}\equiv X\pmod f\) holds exactly when \(f\) is squarefree and every irreducible factor degree divides \(n\).

edges.label: Interpret exclusion tests
edges.explanation: The gcd at \(n/\ell\) is one exactly when no irreducible factor degree divides \(n/\ell\).

edges.label: Divisibility condition
edges.explanation: This condition supplies squarefreeness as well as the allowable factor degrees.

edges.label: All exclusion conditions
edges.explanation: Every prime divisor of the total degree must be checked, without omitting a gcd test.

edges.label: Rabin criterion
edges.explanation: The conjunction rules out every proper factor degree, and every irreducible polynomial passes all these tests.

edges.label: Maximal principal ideal
edges.explanation: The quotient \(\mathbb F_q[X]/(f)\) is a field exactly when \(f\) is irreducible, and then it has \(q^n\) elements.

edges.label: Compute in the quotient
edges.explanation: Repeated modular powering evaluates the final congruence without expanding the enormous Frobenius power.

edges.label: Residues and gcd certificates
edges.explanation: The same modular powers supply each gcd input; the Euclidean algorithm certifies the required coprimality.

sources.locator: §1, Lemma 1 and proof, printed pp. 7–8; quotient construction p. 6
sources.note: The report states the lemma over a prime field. The same subfield argument gives the displayed prime-power version; the proof is included below.
Earlier author report of the work published as Rabin (1980), SIAM Journal on Computing 9, 273–280.

body:
The complete criterion is

\[f\text{ irreducible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\begin{cases}X^{q^n}\equiv X\pmod f,\\[2pt]\gcd\!\left(f,X^{q^{n/\ell}}-X\right)=1&\text{for every prime }\ell\mid n.\end{cases}\]

Here is the proof for arbitrary prime powers, extending the identical prime-field argument in Rabin’s original report. The roots of \(X^{q^m}-X\) form \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\); its derivative is \(-1\). Consequently it is the product, once each, of the monic irreducible polynomials over \(\mathbb F_q\) whose degrees divide \(m\). The first congruence therefore makes \(f\) squarefree with all factor degrees dividing \(n\). If a proper factor degree \(d\mid n\) occurred, choose a prime \(\ell\mid n/d\). Then \(d\mid n/\ell\), contradicting that gcd test. Conversely, an irreducible degree-\(n\) polynomial passes both conditions.

No preliminary squarefreeness assumption is needed. For \(n=1\), the empty gcd list causes no exception. All powers may be reduced modulo \(f\) throughout.

For \(f=X^4+X+1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\), the relation \(X^4\equiv X+1\) gives \(X^8\equiv X^2+1\) and \(X^{16}\equiv X\). The only prime divisor of four is two, and \(X^4-X\equiv1\pmod f\). These computations certify irreducibility and realize the field with sixteen elements as \(\mathbb F_2[X]/(f)\).
